blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.

FOL-Proof的操作方法是通过语义分析工具,如英语资源语法和最小回溯语义等,确定获得一个候选翻译集合;然后应用一个SMT解析器来检查所衍生的每个读取与LLM生成的公式的逻辑等同. 如果译名是忠实的,则被接受;否则就被拒绝,或者通过反复引用LLM来选择修复. 程序是保守的:搜索不全,没有支持的构建,或者没有定论的检查结果为弃权而不是虚假的拒绝. 我们根据既定基准(ProofWriter、RulesTaker和PrOntoQA)以及新的对抗性基准(LongFaithCheck)评估了FOL-Proof。 我们的实验显示,FOL-Proof的精确度接近完美的选择性,而直接的LLM判断和回程基线则显示性能差得多。

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities
across a wide range of natural language processing tasks, including
machine translation, text summarization and question
answering [ 83 , 80 , 22 ] . They
have also shown promising results in reasoning tasks, including
mathematical problem solving, code generation, and logical
inference [ 20 , 84 , 6 ] .

Despite these advances, when it comes to deductive tasks (i.e., deciding whether a conclusion is entailed by given premises), LLMs do not guarantee sound reasoning [ 81 , 54 , 13 ] .
They are prone to many logical fallacies: fabricating axioms, violating the rules of conditional logic, and employing circular logic [ 50 , 24 , 61 , 65 , 27 ] .
For example, consider the reasoning problem in Figure 1 (a). The correct logical answer is that the conclusion is not entailed—Bob is not necessarily a student. But an LLM might conclude otherwise by fabricating an axiom or affirming the consequent.

neural baselines across a spectrum of logical
domains [ 68 , 77 , 3 , 56 , 5 ] .

sentence does not prove that it is faithful to the original,
natural-language sentence; and indeed,
prior work has shown that LLMs frequently mistranslate natural-language statements. Models may select the wrong quantifier or quantifier scope, drop or invert a negation, misuse logical connectives (as is demonstrated in Figure 1 (b)), omit premises or predicates, or even introduce clauses that are not supported by the source text [ 74 , 71 , 30 , 45 ] . In such cases,
the solver may reach the wrong conclusion, due to being fed incorrect

Therefore, the neuro-symbolic approach does not eliminate the
potential for incorrect reasoning when using LLMs, but rather moves
the problem to the auto-formalization stage.

Here, we propose a novel approach: derive a set of formal
interpretations from an independent, linguistically grounded semantic
analysis of the source sentence; and then use these interpretations as
references against which a proposed formalization is checked. Checking
is performed by evaluating logical equivalence using an SMT solver.
We hypothesize that this checking can retain only high-fidelity
translations for downstream reasoning, filtering out formalizations
that are not licensed by the linguistic analysis before they reach the
solver, thus improving logical reasoning (see
Figure 1 (c)).
We term this technique FOL-Proof .

In order to improve the soundness of our approach, we deliberately
designed FOL-Proof to be conservative. It certifies a candidate when some
deterministically derived reading is equivalent to it, and rejects it conclusively only when
the search over parses and scope readings is provably complete and every
adaptable reading is non-equivalent. In all other cases (incomplete search,
unsupported constructions, inconclusive equivalence checks) it abstains, so
resource bounds are never mistaken for semantic
disagreement.

For our implementation of FOL-Proof, we combine the English Resource
Grammar (ERG) [ 17 , 16 ] , Minimal
Recursion Semantics (MRS) [ 9 ] , and a scope
resolution tool [ 31 ] to generate the pool of
candidate translations. We use a deterministic MRS-to-FOL adapter to
translate these references into formulas, and apply the Z3 SMT
solver [ 11 ] to check equivalence between them and the
LLM-based translation being considered. MRS is useful
for this purpose because it can represent semantic structure while
leaving certain scope choices underspecified; these alternatives can
subsequently be resolved rather than prematurely be collapsed into a
single logical formula, thus preserving natural language ambiguities.

blocks.en:
Our evaluation shows that FOL-Proof provides highly reliable semantic
validation across three well-established reasoning benchmarks with
thousands of items, as well as on a new benchmark that we
present here, consisting of adversarial instances. We evaluate
FOL-Proof on controlled mutations and LLM translations, and find that
it achieves near perfect accuracy across tens of thousands of
formalizations, outperforming direct LLM judges and
round-trip baselines. In addition, it accounts for ambiguity and accepts multiple valid translations.
When used as a gate for downstream reasoning,
FOL-Proof attains 100% selective accuracy on all answered
problems. Moreover, incorporating FOL-Proof into an
iterative repair loop improves repair rates from 4.8% to 22.8% when providing feedback, and increasing to 62.6% when exposing the closest licensed reading.

blocks.en: To summarize, this paper makes the following contributions: 1. We propose a novel approach to verifying LLM auto-formalizations into FOL by certifying them against deterministic English parses. 2. We develop FOL-Proof, an implementation of the above approach. 3. We introduce a new benchmark designed to challenge LLMs’ auto-formalization and judging capabilities. 4. We evaluate FOL-Proof on controlled semantic mutations, LLM translations, end-to-end reasoning and a repair loop, and compare it with direct LLM judges and round-trip validators on ProofWriter [ 69 ] , PrOntoQA [ 63 ] , RuleTaker [ 8 ] , and our new benchmark. We find that our approach can establish near perfect accuracy when it does not abstain.

Given a ground-truth (GT) formula (i.e., a correct
translation, used as a point of reference), there exist different
approaches for comparing the candidate translation against it,
typically tailored to the domain of the formula in question.
String metrics such as BLEU are brittle under renaming
and reordering [ 70 , 74 ] . Solver-based approaches instead decide equivalence by
refuting ¬ ( ϕ ↔ ψ ) \neg(\phi\leftrightarrow\psi) with an SMT solver or
ATP [ 49 , 64 ] . Other methods exist for comparing Lean statements [ 39 ] or temporal logic [ 58 ] . When a metric is needed beyond simple equivalence, some methods employ graph distance calculations [ 51 , 42 ] .
These methods are exact or graded with
respect to the GT, but are also limited with respect to that GT: they cannot account for ambiguity, and are inapplicable
when no GT is provided.
In FOL-Proof we also use a negated bi-implication check (Sect. 4.5 ),
but do not assume we are provided with a GT; instead, we use a set of
grammar-licensed readings.

blocks.en:
Natural language sentences often do not entail a unique logical
representation. Specifically, quantifier scope and attachment
standard are sources of ambiguity [ 9 , 31 ] .

代表权。 具体地说,限定范围和附件
标准是模糊性的来源[9、31]。

blocks.en: Consider the sentence “Every student saw a teacher with a telescope” . The prepositional phrase with a telescope creates attachment scope ambiguity. It can attach either to the verb phrase ( saw with a telescope ) or to the noun phrase ( a teacher with a telescope ). Additionally, the quantifier scope is undetermined: is there a single teacher that all the students saw, or did every student see a teacher, but not necessarily the same one.

Grammar (ERG) [ 17 ] , a broad-coverage,
hand-engineered Head-Driven Phrase Structure Grammar
(HPSG) [ 55 ] . The ERG admits multiple MRS analyses for individual sentences, accounting for attachment ambiguity and lexical ambiguity. So, in the case of Example 1 , we would receive separate MRS analyses for the different attachment and lexical ambiguities.

语法(ERG)[17], 广泛覆盖,

blocks.en: Our use of MRS is not intended as a return to traditional grammar-based translation, but rather as a means of complementing modern LLMs with an independent, linguistically grounded semantic analysis. and sometimes formalize controlled linguistic patterns differently. For example, RuleTaker [ 8 ] represents “the cat” as the constant Cat , whereas PrOntoQA [ 63 ] uses Cat(x) as a class predicate.

domain: the selected profile parameterizes the “FOL Adapter” step, while scope resolution and the recursive IR-to-FOL
compiler remain shared. Profile-specific interpretation steps are
recorded in the certificate. The profiles used here are summarized in
Appendix 0.C .

blocks.en: 6.2 Semantic Discrimination and Mutation Detection
blocks.zh: 6.2 语义歧视和变异检测

blocks.en: We begin by running FOL-Proof on the gold-certified translations of ProofWriter, RuleTaker, PrOntoQA and LongFaithCheck. We find that FOL-Proof correctly accepts 100% of candidates on RuleTaker, PrOntoQA and LongFaithCheck. On ProofWriter, FOL-Proof correctly accepts 6,262 cases (77.80%) and abstains on the rest, due to unsupported_semantics and parse_search_incomplete .

We test whether validators reject formulas that differ from a correct
translation by a single controlled semantic edit (relation-argument reversal,
negation addition or removal, implication reversal, antecedent deletion,
quantifier swap, and constant or predicate substitution). On ProofWriter, we generated 21,584
such mutations from 4,297 certified correct parents, 25,881 instances in total. On PrOntoQA, we generated 27,255 such mutations from 9,494 certified correct parents, 36,749 instances in total.
In both panels, Z3 independently confirmed that
every mutation is non-equivalent to its source formula.
FOL-Proof reached 100% accuracy and 100% balanced accuracy on both panels (Table 1 ).
In contrast, the baselines lagged behind: On ProofWriter, the best baseline is the Qwen direct judge, with
94.90% accuracy and 89.0% balanced accuracy: it rejects 97.8% of
mutations but accepts only 80.1% of correct parents.
Among Qwen round-trip gates, the best was Monty clausal coverage, with 80.81%
accuracy.
On PrOntoQA, the strongest baseline is Qwen Monty clausal coverage,
with 97.58% accuracy and 97.60% balanced accuracy; the Qwen direct
judge reaches 97.45% accuracy and 96.53% balanced accuracy.
Additional results for selected configurations
appear in Appendix Table 8 .

blocks.en: Table 1 reports pooled results over all 2,000 pairs. FOL-Proof decided every case and agreed with the benchmark label on all of them: it certified all 1,000 correct translations and conclusively rejected all 1,000 mutated ones, with no abstentions. The learned baselines are far weaker, and no baseline exceeds 74.4% accuracy. The best direct judge (Qwen) gets there almost entirely through acceptance bias, accepting 98.8% of correct pairs but rejecting only 49.9% of mutated ones. The round-trip gates show the opposite failure: most reject conservatively and recover few correct translations. Direct judges and round-trip gates therefore err in complementary directions rather than discriminating faithful from unfaithful translations. Besides evaluating FOL-Proof’s effectiveness at catching wrong translations, this experiment demonstrates that LongFaithCheck is more challenging for LLM judges than the other benchmarks.
blocks.zh: 表1报告所有2 000对成果的汇总情况。 FOL-Proof决定了每个案件,同意所有案件的基准标签:它认证了所有1 000种正确的翻译,并最后否决了所有1 000种变异翻译,没有弃权。 学到的基线要弱得多,基准的准确度不超过74.4%。 最好的直接裁判(Quen)几乎完全通过接受偏差到达,接受98.8%的正确配对,但只拒绝49.9%的变异配对. 圆通门显示相反的失败:大多数都保守地拒绝,并收回很少正确的翻译. 因此,直接法官和往返审判门在辅助方向上是错误的,而不是歧视忠实者不忠的翻译。 除了评价FOL-Proof在获取错误翻译方面的有效性外,这项实验还表明,LongFaithCheck对LLM法官而言比其他基准更具挑战性。

Against the licensed-normalized reference used in Table 2 , 692 outputs (23.1%) are positive, so a validator that rejects everything scores 76.9%. We therefore focus on balanced accuracy and on the error counts.

blocks.en: Table 2 compares validators on LLM-generated translations. FOL-Proof agrees with the licensed-normalized reference on 99.7% of the 3,000 LongFaithCheck outputs, 99.7% on PrOntoQA, 99.9% on RuleTaker and 100% on ProofWriter. Even when the best single model is chosen per family and per benchmark, no learned baseline comes close in balanced accuracy: the strongest reaches 63.9% on LongFaithCheck, 73.4% on PrOntoQA, 81.9% on RuleTaker and 86.0% on ProofWriter. The failure modes remain complementary: direct judges accept almost everything (on LongFaithCheck the Mistral and Phi judges accept 97.8% and 96.2% of correct translations but reject only 4.8% and 10.5% of incorrect ones), while the stricter round-trip gates reject almost everything and barely beat a validator that rejects every translation. Detailed results are in Appendix 0.F : LongFaithCheck per-model results in Table 9 , and the complete cross-benchmark configurations in Table 10 . A secondary result is that LongFaithCheck is harder for these LLMs to translate (23.1% of generated translations match the licensed-normalized reference, versus 66.1%–73.6% on ProofWriter, RuleTaker, and PrOntoQA), consistent with its intended purpose.

A crucial observation comes from analyzing the source of FOL-Proof’s imperfect accuracy. On RuleTaker, FOL-Proof abstains on 11 parse-incomplete
items. On LongFaithCheck and PrOntoQA, all the disagreements with the gold
certificate are false accepts (10 and 42 respectively).
The residual disagreements are highly structured:
On LongFaithCheck, the ten false accepts collapse into two templates. In the first, sentences of the form “Some A A R R every B B ”
were certified under the inverse-scope reading ∀ y ⁡ ( B ⁡ ( y ) → ∃ x ⁡ ( A ⁡ ( x ) ∧ R ⁡ ( x , y ) ) ) \forall y(B(y)\rightarrow\exists x(A(x)\land R(x,y))) , rather than the

This is a well-attested ambiguity of doubly quantified English sentences:
experimental work treats examples such as “A girl saw every boy” as

The remaining five LongFaithCheck cases involve a less preferred, but still
systematically generated, interaction between existential quantification and
negation. Sentences of the form “Some A A is/does not P P ” were licensed as ¬ ∃ ⁡ x ⁡ ( A ⁡ ( x ) ∧ P ⁡ ( x ) ) \neg\exists x(A(x)\land P(x)) , equivalently ∀ x ⁡ ( A ⁡ ( x ) → ¬ P ⁡ ( x ) ) \forall x(A(x)\rightarrow\neg P(x)) , instead of the reference ∃ x ⁡ ( A ⁡ ( x ) ∧ ¬ P ⁡ ( x ) ) \exists x(A(x)\land\neg P(x)) . This is not an arbitrary corruption of the
formula: it corresponds to a coherent scope ordering produced by the
linguistic analysis. However, psycholinguistic and semantic work indicates that the reference benchmark reading is generally
the interpretation speakers assign to the sentence [ 37 , 67 , 14 ] .
Thus these five cases illustrate a boundary between grammatical scope
generation and human interpretive preference: FOL-Proof certifies a
compositionally coherent reading, but one that speakers would not ordinarily
intend in the benchmark context. An analogous phenomenon explains all 42 false accepts on PrOntoQA, see Appendix 0.F.4 . If we treat these cases as genuine ambiguity, the accuracy of FOL-Proof on both benchmarks rises to 100%.

To evaluate the impact of semantic validation on downstream
reasoning, we use FOL-Proof as a gate between an LLM-based
translator and a deterministic symbolic reasoner.
Each premise and query is validated independently, and a
reasoning problem is processed only if all its translations
are certified. The resulting formulas are then passed to
a Horn-rule reasoning component [ 43 ] that derives conclusions
through forward chaining over a supported logical fragment.
We evaluated downstream deduction across ProofWriter, PrOntoQA, and RuleTaker benchmarks.
Table 3 compares selection policies when a deterministic
reasoner answers the questions. All policies use the same
whole-problem availability rule: a question is answered only if its query and
every premise compiled under that policy. The strict policy additionally
requires every one of them to be certified. It was correct on every question it
answered in all three benchmarks. The price is coverage: one
uncertified premise blocks the whole problem, so strict yield is 25.5%, 70.2%,
and 56.7%. In summary, when FOL-Proof is used as a gate for translations, the resulting answers have 100.0% accuracy .

blocks.en: We evaluated validator-guided repair on 500 LongFaithCheck translations rejected as not_derivable , allowing up to three repair attempts per case (Table 4 ). Blind regeneration succeeded in only 4.8% of cases, whereas supplying FOL-Proof’s compact diagnostic increased certification to 22.8%. These results demonstrate that verifier-derived diagnostics can guide semantic correction, although their effectiveness remains limited.
blocks.zh: 我们评价了500名LongFaithCheck译文的校验者指导修复, 盲人再生只成功4.8%,而提供FOL-Proof的紧凑诊断则将认证提高到22.8%。 这些结果表明,从核查者获得的诊断可以指导语义矫正,尽管其有效性仍然有限。

blocks.en: A substantially higher certification rate (62.6%) was achieved by exposing licensed readings. This condition can be understood as semantic projection : rather than supplying an arbitrary reference, FOL-Proof identifies a Pareto-optimal frontier of licensed interpretations closest to the model’s original candidate under structural distance measures, providing targets for semantic alignment. Since these readings are independently derived from the source sentence, no benchmark ground-truth formulas are required. While this setting does not isolate the LLM’s ability to correct errors without explicit semantic targets, it demonstrates the potential of combining deterministic semantic analysis with LLM-guided revision. Additional feedback, including solver countermodels, yielded no further improvement (61.6%).
blocks.zh: 通过披露有许可证的读数,认证率大大提高(62.6%)。 这个条件可以被理解为语义投射:FOL-Proof不是提供任意的参考,而是在结构距离度量下确定一个最接近模型原始候选方的许可解释的Pareto-优化前沿,为语义对齐提供了目标. 由于这些读数是独立来源于源句,因此不需要基准地面真实公式. 虽然这种设置并不孤立LLM在没有明确语义目标的情况下纠正错误的能力,但它显示了将确定语义分析与LLM制导修订相结合的潜力. 其他反馈,包括解析器反模型,没有产生进一步的改进(61.6%).

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion and Future Work
blocks.zh: 7 结论和今后的工作

blocks.en:
We presented FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall for validating LLM-generated
first-order logic translations against independently derived linguistic analyses.
Rather than asking another language model to judge a translation, FOL-Proof
derives candidate readings from the ERG/MRS analysis of the source sentence,
compiles supported readings deterministically into FOL, and certifies a
candidate only when model-theoretic equivalence can be established, abstaining
rather than rejecting when the evidence is incomplete.

对照独立衍生的语言分析进行一阶逻辑翻译.
FOL-Proof 与其要求另一个语言模型来判断翻译,不如请另一个语言模型来判断翻译。
从ERG/MRS对源句的分析中得出候选读数,

只有在模式理论等同性能够确定时,才予以候选,弃权
而不是在证据不完整时拒绝。

blocks.en:
Empirically, FOL-Proof achieves near perfect selective accuracy on controlled semantic mutations and on gold-certified translations once scope ambiguities are accounted for. On LLM-generated translations across ProofWriter, RuleTaker, PrOntoQA and the adversarial LongFaithCheck benchmark it reaches near-100% agreement with licensed-normalized references and outperforms direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines, whose complementary failure modes (over-acceptance versus over-rejection) leave a large residual error. When certificates are used to select premises and queries for downstream deduction, selective accuracy reaches 100% on every answered problem. Finally, the repair study shows that independently derived validator feedback can raise certification from 4.8% under blind regeneration to 22.8%, and 62.6% when complete
formulas for selected licensed readings were also exposed, within
three repair attempts.
blocks.zh:
经验是,FOL-Proof在可控语义变异和黄金认证翻译方面,一旦考虑到范围模糊性,就几乎实现了完美的选择性精确。 在LLM生成的跨ProofWriter、RuleTaker、PrOntoQA和对抗性LongFaithCheck基准的翻译上,它与获得许可的正常引用达成近100%的协议,并且超越了直接的LLM法官和往返基准,其互补的失败模式(过度接受与过度拒绝)留下了巨大的剩余错误。 当证书用于选择房地和查询以进行下游扣减时,在每个被回答的问题上,选择性精确度达到100%. 最后,修复研究显示,独立产生的验证器反馈可提高认证率,从盲目再生的4.8%提高到22.8%,如完成则提高到62.6%。

blocks.en: Several limitations remain, suggesting directions for future work. First, the current adapters cover only a controlled fragment of English. We plan to investigate algorithmic transfer of semantic composition rules from related formalisms—particularly Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) [ 66 ] and its compositional semantics—into the existing MRS-to-FOL pipeline. Second, scope enumeration remains combinatorial, and long sentences can generate thousands of parses and factorially many scope trees, making exhaustive search impractical under tight resource bounds. We will develop algorithmic improvements for pruning parse forests and accelerating scope search, through incremental equivalence checking that aborts a reading as soon as a counter-model is found, and caching of intermediate Semantic-IR fragments across related analyses. Third, repair feedback, while already effective, still leaves a substantial fraction of cases uncertified after the budget is exhausted. Richer, more actionable feedback should raise success rates further.
blocks.zh: 仍然存在一些局限性,为今后的工作提出了方向。 首先,目前的适配器只覆盖英语的一个可控片段. 我们计划调查将语义组成规则从有关的形式主义——特别是组合分类语法[66]及其组成语义——向现有的MRS到FOL管道的算法转移。 第二,范围查点仍然是组合式的,冗长的句子可以产生上千个剖面和因数上的许多范围树,使得在严格的资源界限下进行详尽的搜索不切实际. 我们将通过增量等值检查,在发现反模型后立即中止读取,并在相关分析中将中间语义-IR片段夹住,从而开发算法改进,以探测剖析森林并加快范围搜索。 第三,修复反馈虽然已经很有效,但在预算用完之后仍有相当一部分案件没有得到核证。 更丰富、更可操作的反馈应进一步提高成功率。

blocks.en:
An MRS consists of a collection of elementary predications
( RELS ) and constraints on their possible scopes
( HCONS ). Each predication has a label
( LBL ), called a handle , identifying its
local semantic position. Predications sharing a label
are interpreted conjunctively. Arguments are variables
denoting entities ( x 1 , x 2 , x 3 x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} ) or events ( e 4 , e 5 e_{4},e_{5} ): ARG0 identifies the variable associated with
the predication, while ARG1 , ARG2 ,
etc. specify semantic roles. For example, _see_v_1 describes an event e 4 e_{4} in which
student x 1 x_{1} sees teacher x 2 x_{2} . The _with_p predication relates that event to
telescope x 3 x_{3} , and shares its label h 13 h_{13} .
The numerical spans (e.g., <14:17> ) identify
the corresponding characters in the input sentence.

Quantifiers additionally introduce two handle-valued
arguments: RSTR , specifying the restriction
(e.g., being a student), and BODY , specifying
the proposition within the quantifier’s scope.
These handles act as holes whose contents are
not yet fully determined. The HCONS constraints
restrict their possible fillings: for example, h2 qeq h4 requires the restriction of every to reach the student predication,
possibly through intervening quantifiers.
The constraint h0 qeq h13 similarly anchors
the sentence’s top handle ( TOP ) to the verbal
predications, without fixing the intervening quantifier
order. The INDEX identifies the main event and
its grammatical features; ICONS , empty here,
would contain additional constraints on individual
variables.

The adapter builds this IR from the roles and scope relations in a
supported tree. It interprets a quantifier’s restriction and body as
separate subexpressions, composes logical operators recursively, and
records the rules used. It then checks for unbound variables before
compilation. If a tree contains a construction for which the selected
profile defines no deterministic interpretation, adaptation reports
that reading as unsupported instead of supplying a formula. The
compiler only lowers an already constructed IR; it does not choose
scope, reinterpret MRS predicates, or apply profile-specific
enrichments.

For 𝙽𝚘𝚝𝙳𝚎𝚛𝚒𝚟𝚊𝚋𝚕𝚎 \mathtt{NotDerivable} outcomes, FOL-Proof can optionally compute, per licensed reading compared, four structural distance measures: complete formula-tree distance (GTED) [ 42 ] , name-masked topology distance [ 13 , 40 ] , predicate-inventory distance [ 73 , 5 ] , and constant-inventory distance [ 5 , 64 ] . These diagnostics localize disagreement between the candidate and a licensed reading—distinguishing differences in logical structure from differences in predicate or entity vocabulary—without interpreting structural similarity as semantic equivalence.
FOL-Proof then selects a bounded Pareto frontier of nearby readings (default 3), and reports reading-relative diagnoses (quantifier/negation/argument-order/implication-direction/constant/predicate/missing-or-extra-literal differences; a single-predicate-substitution diagnosis is reported only when it suffices to make the full candidate identical to the selected reading). Four disclosure levels gate what is exposed downstream: off , components (structural differences only), readings (adds the selected licensed formulas and normalized candidate), full (adds structured, possibly partially-evaluated Z3 countermodels, marked evaluation_complete=false where relevant). This machinery is diagnostic only.

The supported English fragment comprises constructions for which the
selected profile supplies a deterministic mapping. The default compact
fragment covers controlled declaratives with properties, binary relations,
quantification, negation, supported conjunction and disjunction graphs, and

discourse-level pronoun resolution, modality, generalized quantifiers, full
temporal semantics, arbitrary ontology alignment, and unrestricted
coordination. The target remains closed, function-free, equality-free FOL.

blocks.en: The direct-judgment baseline prompted the three models with only the English sentence and candidate FOL formula; each returned an ACCEPT or REJECT decision. Missing or unparsable decisions were treated as abstentions. The VeriTrans-style baseline accepts candidates when pairwise TF-IDF cosine similarity between the original and reconstructed English reaches 0.75 0.75 [ 41 ] ; the Monty-style baseline applies a 0.60 0.60 threshold to coverage of the source’s substantive clauses without added content [ 38 ] . A formal-cycle baseline independently translates FOL to English and back to FOL, then checks equivalence of the formal endpoints using alpha equivalence or Z3, adapting closed-loop verification [ 29 ] . We additionally score bidirectional English entailment with BART-MNLI and a combined gate requiring both entailment and formal equivalence, following the round-trip analysis of [ 2 ] . Each gate is evaluated for three independently run models and as a model-majority diagnostic motivated by consensus-based verification [ 64 ] . These baselines adapt the cited methods to our fixed NL–FOL candidates; they are not exact reproductions of the original systems.

blocks.en:
This subsection examines the 42 residual PrOntoQA cases in which
FOL-Proof accepts a candidate that disagrees with the benchmark
reference. All have the surface form “ A A s are not B B ”. The
benchmark reference is ∀ x ⁡ ( A ⁡ ( x ) → ¬ B ⁡ ( x ) ) \forall x(A(x)\rightarrow\neg B(x)) , whereas the ERG-derived reading
matched by the candidate is ¬ ∀ ⁡ x ⁡ ( A ⁡ ( x ) → B ⁡ ( x ) ) \neg\forall x(A(x)\rightarrow B(x)) , equivalently ∃ x ⁡ ( A ⁡ ( x ) ∧ ¬ B ⁡ ( x ) ) \exists x(A(x)\land\neg B(x)) .

In every case the candidate matches a scope-resolved formula derived
by the ERG/MRS pipeline, so the certificate is faithful to that
analysis. The disagreement concerns which negation-scope analysis
best captures the intended reading of the bare-plural sentence.
English bare plurals have generic and scope behavior distinct from
overtly quantified noun phrases [ 7 , 33 ] ;
in ordinary usage, however, “ A A s are not B B ” is normally
understood as a generic or universal negative rather than the weaker
claim that some A A is not B B . We therefore treat these cases as
systematic reading-preference conflicts: the ERG-derived translations
are formally licensed, but differ from the reading normally intended
in this controlled benchmark.
